coredata.dc:description: Lignin can be used as a sustainable alternative to bisphenol A (BPA) to prepared lignin-based epoxy resins. Lignin effects including molecular weight, phenolic content, G/S unit ratio and flexible/rigid linkage ratio on epoxy synthesis and performance were summarized comprehensively. The incorporation of lignin with a higher molecular weight would lead to the higher rigidity of epoxy crosslinking network. Higher contents of ether bonds in lignin would provide higher structural flexibility of lignin incorporated epoxy thermosets. Lignin with higher contents of phenolic hydroxyls was more beneficial for improving the reactivity of its epoxy products after glycidylation. Due to the excellent charring capacity of lignin, higher contents of residue char can be produced at higher additions of lignin at high temperatures, while the loss of crosslinking density caused by the increasing lignin addition (especially for the macromolecular lignin) would deteriorate the thermal stability of their thermosets. Several applications of lignin-based epoxy resins were also mentioned based on their mechanical, thermal and chemical properties, such as coatings (with anticorrosion and UV-blocking), adhesives (with highly crosslinking network, excellent mechanical, and thermal properties) and flame retardants (with high charring capability).

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Lignin can be used as a sustainable alternative to bisphenol A (BPA) to prepared lignin-based epoxy resins. Lignin effects including molecular weight, phenolic content, G/S unit ratio and flexible/rigid linkage ratio on epoxy synthesis and performance were summarized comprehensively. The incorporation of lignin with a higher molecular weight would lead to the higher rigidity of epoxy crosslinking network. Higher contents of ether bonds in lignin would provide higher structural flexibility of lignin incorporated epoxy thermosets. Lignin with higher contents of phenolic hydroxyls was more beneficial for improving the reactivity of its epoxy products after glycidylation. Due to the excellent charring capacity of lignin, higher contents of residue char can be produced at higher additions of lignin at high temperatures, while the loss of crosslinking density caused by the increasing lignin addition (especially for the macromolecular lignin) would deteriorate the thermal stability of their thermosets. Several applications of lignin-based epoxy resins were also mentioned based on their mechanical, thermal and chemical properties, such as coatings (with anticorrosion and UV-blocking), adhesives (with highly crosslinking network, excellent mechanical, and thermal properties) and flame retardants (with high charring capability).

ce:section.ce:para: Contributing the most abundant natural aromatic polymer in the Earth, lignin is composed of three phenylpropane units including guaiacyl (G-type lignin), syringyl (S-type lignin) and p-hydroxyphenyl (H-type lignin) [1–3]. Lignin can be extracted from lignocellulose (e.g., from forestry and agricultural residues) or black liquor (e.g., from pulping and papermaking mills) and is considered as a by-product with low-utilization rate [4,5]. It is an urgent requirement but a big challenge to achieve valuable applications of lignin. One effective pathway is lignin depolymerization to produce aromatic monomers [6–8]. In 2019, Dong et al. broke the production limitation of aromatic monomers via effective CC bonds cleavage of lignin over Ru/NbOP4 catalyst to harvest 153 % monocyclic C6-C9 hydrocarbons [9]. However, the complex mixture of depolymerized lignin compounds makes the subsequent separation, purification, and further applications more difficult. During depolymerization, the rigid structure of lignin is proposed to be a major obstacle to achieve its efficient conversion, and also the depolymerized mechanism is hard to be investigated clearly majorly due to the ambiguous lignin structure extracted from wide ranges of biomass materials [10]. Reversely, due to the inherent crosslinking structure, lignin can be used by nature to give strength and rigidity to the plant cell walls [11,12], hence it has potential to be applied as a reinforcement material to improve the mechanical properties of polymer composites [13], such as bio-based thermoplastic or thermosetting materials [14,15]. On the other hand, with the increasing demand of sustainable development, green chemistry has arisen as a popular way in the synthesis of polymers or other materials due to the negative outlook provided by traditional fossil-derived resources, and the utilization of natural resources as raw materials is good fit for green chemistry [16,17].

Epoxy resins, as a highly reactive pre-polymer containing epoxy groups, can be reacted to form cross-linked macromolecular compounds via either self-homo-polymerization or curing reaction with other co-reactants (such as amines, anhydrides and other acids, alcohols, esters) [18–20]. Among them, curing reactions of epoxy resins can form epoxy thermosets containing excellent mechanical, thermal and chemical stability, endowing them with wide applications such as coatings, adhesives, electric insulators, polymeric reinforced materials and paintbrushes [21,22]. However, the most used epoxy resin (over 90 % of epoxy monomer/pre-polymer production) is the type of diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA), of which the synthesis is mainly based on bisphenol A (BPA, which is mainly produced from fossil-derived resources, and its wide utilization greatly poses a threat to the environment and human health) [23,24]. In foster and promote sustainability, exploring the renewable alternative has become a hotspot of intensive research [25]. Lignin, due to its abundance, sustainability, and inherent polyphenolic structure, has been regarded as a promisingly renewable alternative for BPA in the preparation of bio-based epoxy resins [26]. Given these backgrounds, lignin-based epoxy resins which are not dependent on fossil resources and are not harmful for the environment and human health attract much attention, which have the great potential to replace fossil-derived ones in the future. A keyword search using “lignin and epoxy resin” was performed to identify the related researching articles for investigation, summary, and comparison. The number of papers relating to lignin-based epoxy resins published in journals from Web of Science from 2001 to 2022 intended to increase, where the number of papers published in the last three years (from 2020 to 2022) was 215, accounting for 2.23 % of the total number of papers on epoxy resins published in the same period. Considering the essential meaning of developing sustainable epoxy resins, although an accurate investigation of the paper number change by keyword search (i.e., lignin and epoxy resin) seems to be limited (e.g., 75 in 2020, 75 in 2021, and 65 in 2022), the study on lignin-based epoxy resins should be highlighted and the number of researching papers focusing on this field would increase at least recently. For recognizing the recent researching trends of lignin-based epoxy resins systematically, the related researching papers were obtained manually from 362 articles using keyword search of “lignin” and “epoxy resin” from 2015 to 2022. The result showed that lignin-based epoxy resins using macromolecular lignin (292, including native and functionalized lignin), depolymerized lignin (51), and lignin model compounds (19) were all collected. Among these collected articles, related reviews (35) were not included, and it is sufficient to review the recent researching trends from these above mentioned articles.

In this review, we introduced that many studies prepared lignin-based epoxy pre-polymers (i.e., glycidylated lignin) directly via epichlorohydrin (ECH) modification. After being blended with DGEBA to achieve partial replacement, such lignin-based epoxy thermosets can be prepared through curing reactions, obtaining improved mechanical and thermal properties. On the other hand, with decreasing molecular weight via lignin structural depolymerization or directly using monomeric model compounds, lignin fragments with low molecular weight can also be used as co-curing agents for epoxy resins. With the higher reactivity of depolymerized lignin to glycidylation, their glycidylated products containing higher epoxy values show positive effects on the synthesis and properties of their thermosets. Due to the lack of active phenolic hydroxyls in monomeric model compounds, certain modifications and/or poly-condensation reactions (to form dimers or even trimers) are employed to promote their accessibility to epoxy pre-polymers preparation. As compared to other related reviews on lignin- (or bio-) based epoxy resins, this review mainly focuses on the changes of epoxy synthesis and then their properties (mechanical and thermal properties) caused by the change of lignin molecular weight. For example, as the same partial replacer of BPA in epoxy synthesis, macromolecular lignin (with or without chemical functionalization) can be used as a reinforcement material due to its crosslinking structure, while low-molecule-weight lignin can be mainly used as a co-curing agent to act as a “bridge” in formed epoxy thermosetting systems, and their related synthesis pathways have been presented in this review. On the other hand, other effects of lignin structure (e.g., phenolic content, S/G ratio, and β-O-4/β-5 ratio) and reaction conditions (e.g., glycidylation degree, lignin content, solvent effect, and catalytic effect) are also summarized in this review, which is more clear and basic for common readers than other related reviews.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Lignin-based epoxy resins and their curing processes
ce:section.ce:para:
Lignin-based epoxy resins can be directly produced from lignin glycidylation (Fig. 1 ), and can be further used to prepare lignin-based epoxy thermosets though curing process by themselves or their composites blended with certain amounts of commercial epoxy resins (e.g., DGEBA, E51 or E44). Several kinds of curing agents can be used to complete epoxy curing reactions, mainly including amines and anhydrides, as well as other kinds of alcohols and acids. Among them, amines (including aromatic and aliphatic amines) are widely used for preparing epoxy thermosets, and their curing reactions are shown in Fig. 1. Additionally, different curing agents would lead to different curing properties, such as curing temperature (T
peak , °C), total heat release (ΔH, J/kg), and/or overall activation energy (E
α , kJ/mol) (Table 1 ). For example, the curing properties of 4,4′-diaminodiphenylmethane (DDM, an aromatic amine curing agent) and diethylenetriamine (DETA, an aliphatic amine curing agent) were investigated, wherein DDM incorporated curing process released more heat and required lower curing activation energy, indicative of the higher reactivity of DDM [27]. The main reason could be the self-curing phenomenon happening in DDM incorporated curing process, while DETA incorporated ones were dominantly controlled by autocatalytic reactions (e.g., etherification or polymerization reactions) with higher activation energy [28–30]. On the other hand, different anhydrides, including maleic anhydride (MA) and methylhexahydrophthalic anhydride (MTHPA), were studied for their curing properties. MA contained higher curing reactivity than MTHPA, which was attributed to the methyl in MTHPA structure, of which the steric hindrance and inductive effect decreased the electrophilic reactivity of carboxylic acid, thus to lower the curing reactivity of MTHPA [31,32].

Lignin, as a natural aromatic biopolymer, has been promisingly used as a green alternative of fossil-derived BPA in epoxy resins production [37]. On the other hand, lignin can also be used as a crosslinking filler in epoxy resins mainly due to its phenolic nature (i.e., phenolic hydroxyls are known to have high reactivity towards epoxy ring open reactions) [38]. To this context, lignin with more content of important phenolic hydroxyls are more desirable as a crosslinking filler [39,40]. However, it is difficult to directly blend lignin with macromolecular structure and epoxy matrix with high compatibility and dispersibility due to the structural stubborness and low reactivity of lignin, which would cause negative effects on physicochemical properties of as-prepared lignin-based thermosetting materials [41,42].

Lignin functionalization would increase the chemical interaction with epoxy resins, such as lignin amination/esterification (the introduction of amine/anhydride groups in lignin structure) [43,44]. Lignin glycidylation to obtain glycidylized lignin with enhanced structural compatibility in epoxy matrix has been proved as a more notable and extensive method [45,46]. For example, Xue et al. fabricated a lignin-based epoxy composite via replacing DGEBA with glycidylated enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (GEL) [47]. The mechanical properties showed that the highest tensile strength (39.5 MPa) but the lowest elongation (5.5 %) were obtained at 100 % lignin addition. It was suggested that an increasing lignin addition would lead to an enhancement of crosslinking density via forming a rigid structure (which would cause the increase of stiffness), while the molecule-chain mobility would be deteriorated due to the enhanced crosslinking density and steric hindrance (which would subsequently result in the decrease of toughness). Thermal properties showed that the thermal stability was improved with the increase of lignin addition due to the inherent thermal stability of lignin.

According to literatures, lignin addition should be controlled because the epoxy composite formed with a high content (e.g., 50 wt%) of lignin was not easy to shape. Furthermore, excessive lignin addition (e.g., > 50 wt%) would cause a deterioration on structural compatibility [47,48]. However, to achieve full replacement of petroleum-derived resources by biomass, Tang et al. fabricated a bio-based epoxy resin using glycidylated lignin and sebacic acid (SA), and investigated lignin structural effects (e.g., molecular weight, phenolic content, S/G ratio, and the ratio of flexible to rigid linkages) on the thermosetting performance (e.g., stiffness, toughness, and thermal stability). The correlations are shown in Table 2 (positive/negative: related performance was improved/deteriorated with the enhancement of such lignin parameters) [49]. Lignin with a lower molecular weight and higher reactivity was beneficial to generate a denser crosslinking epoxy network with better mechanical properties [50], while its thermal stability showed an opposite trend due to the loss of lignin structural rigidity [51]. The increase of S/G ratio in lignin was disadvantageous for crosslinking density due to more H and G units were possibly presented in lignin fractions with low molecular weight [49]. More S-type units in lignin structure (e.g., hardwood lignin) benefited the flexibility, while more C5-condensed aromatic structure would be formed from G-type units in lignin (e.g., softwood lignin), thus reducing molecular mobility and increasing structural rigidity [52]. The phenolic content showed the same trend as that of flexible/rigid linkages ratio (ether/C-C bonds) due to the higher content of phenolic hydroxyls would lead to more ether bonds and flexible structures, suggesting that their enhancements would benefit the tensile properties, but deteriorate thermal stability.

Except lignin effects (lignin structure and its addition), other parameters (e.g., self-condensation reaction and catalytic effects) would also influence the epoxy synthesis. Jablonskis et al. fabricated a lignin-based epoxy resin through two synthesis pathways (i: initial lignin extraction using acetone → glycidylation; ii: initial lignin glycidylation → acetone extraction) with different yields and epoxy values [48]. It was evident that due to the poor dispersion, the self-condensation between lignin and glycidylated lignin would happen (Fig. 2 ) to decrease the yield of acetone-extraction epoxy phase through pathway ii. Owing to the excellent solubility both for acetone extracted lignin and glycidylated lignin fraction in acetone, self-condensation was efficiently avoided through pathway i. In addition, the catalytic effect on lignin glycidylation reactions (including hydroxyl ionization and oxirane ring formation) was proposed through a lignin model compound (i.e., vanillyl alcohol, containing both phenolic and aliphatic hydroxyls). Among all hydroxyls (from phenolic, aliphatic and carboxylic groups), phenolic hydroxyl was the most accessible for glycidylation [53]. The increasing content of alkali catalysts (e.g., NaOH/KOH) was beneficial for the enhancement of glycidylation reactions and the content of diglycidylated ethers proportionally increased with the increase of TBAB addition (a phase transfer catalyst) [54]. Therefore, the biphasic phase transfer catalyst system (e.g., KOH(NaOH)/TBAB) can be a promising catalytic system and has been widely applied to improve lignin glycidylation [51,55–57].

In summary, Fig. 3 shows the related parameter effects on the synthesis and properties of lignin-based epoxy materials. Due to the branched, cross-linked and/or the high-molecule structure of lignin, its incorporation into DGEBA (with lower molecule and linear structure) would lead to the increase of the intrinsic fraction between fluids' molecules. The complete glycidylation of all hydroxyl moieties would greatly improve the compatibility in DGEBA, thus to improve the mechanical properties in terms of both stiffness and toughness. Due to the physical reinforcement of lignin, low contents of lignin blending exhibited positive effects on crosslinking density and mechanical properties. However, the higher lignin addition with more rigid structure was disadvantageous for the flexibility (toughness, determined by flexible components, such as the long-chain amine curing agent or ether bonds in lignin structure) of lignin-based thermosetting materials due to the predominant proportion of rigid components and the deteriorated mobility of molecular chains. For the thermal stability, a slightly lower starting degradation temperature would be observed after lignin incorporation compared to that of reference resin, due to the intra-chain dehydration (or assigned as primary condensation) of free hydroxyls in lignin structure before 300 °C [58]. A higher temperature (over 300 °C) was favorable for the formation of thermostable aromatics with condensed and highly cross-linked structures. The maximum degradation temperature would decrease with the increase of lignin addition due to the deteriorated crosslinking density. However, the final char residue content was proportional to lignin addition, illustrating the important function of lignin as a charcoal formation promoter [59]. Glycidylation conditions should also be designed carefully to adjust the modified lignin structure and hydroxyls conversion. Therefore, biphasic PTC (KOH/NaOH-TBAB) should be considered for improving lignin glycidylation. In addition, solvent effect should also be considered for effectively dispersing lignin phases before/after glycidylation to avoid self-condensation.

Lignin is a result of structural polymerization of three aromatic alcohols (i.e., p-coumaryl/H-units, coniferyl/G-units, and sinapyl/S-units) [60]. These phenylpropane monolignols indicate that lignin can be depolymerized into phenolic products (e.g., monomers, dimers, or trimers), which can be promisingly used as novel types of bio-based resources for certain industries (e.g., epoxy resins production). Recently, lignin can be in-situ depolymerized during the biomass fractionation or reductive catalytic fractionation. As compared to macromolecular lignin without any treatments, depolymerized lignin with lower molecular weight would exhibit higher reactivity and functionality for both lignin glycidylation and curing reactions (where lignin acted as a high-reactive phenolic co-curing agent), and the subsequently prepared lignin-based epoxy thermosets would present better physicochemical properties [61].

For biomass fractionation, Asada et al. performed steam explosion to treat raw lignocellulosic biomass, followed by methanol extraction to isolate low-molecular lignin fragments (Mw: 1330 to 1600 g/mol) with high purity (> 99.0 %) and hydroxyl equivalent (115–118 g/eq), which were used for lignin glycidylation and further purification. These low-molecular lignin fractions were employed as phenolic co-curing agents to EP828/glycidylated lignin epoxy composites for preparing lignin-based epoxy thermosetting composites [57]. As for their thermal decomposition properties, due to phenols detachment at ⁓ 270 °C, and intra-chain dehydration/primary condensation of free hydroxyls or methoxy decomposition (releasing methanol and/or CO2) at ⁓ 380 °C, the thermal decomposition temperature at initial stages (100–300, 300–500 °C) decreased [58,62]. After lignin depolymerization, more content of phenolic hydroxyls would be obtained from the cleavage of ether bonds [63,64]. Therefore, depolymerized lignin was also used as bio-based curing agents for epoxy resins [65]. During the curing process, phenolic hydroxyl in lignin can be reacted with epoxy via polymerization, which is similar to the mechanism of self-condensation during lignin glycidylation [48]. Hydroxyl equivalent in lignin would be a key parameter, and the pre-consumption of phenolic hydroxyls caused by the formation of polyphenolic structure would be disadvantageous for curing reactions. For curing characteristics and activation energy, Ferdosian et al. found that [66], as compared to the commercial DGEBA, the initial curing temperature of depolymerized lignin-based epoxy resins increased slightly due to their higher viscosity restricting the curing reaction, and their lower epoxy contents led to the lower total curing heating and the higher activation energy. In addition, the activation energy of glycidylated lignin increased with the extent of curing reaction due to self-condensation [29]. Zhang et al. found that as compared to raw lignin with cross-linked structure (with Mw = 11,700 g/mol), depolymerized lignin fragments (with Mw = 1400 g/mol) exhibited the higher reactivity as a co-curing agent in epoxy curing reactions via lowering curing temperature and activation energy [67]. Furthermore, depolymerized lignin-based epoxy thermosets showed better mechanical properties compared to those cured with raw lignin, indicative of the importance of lignin molecular weight in structural properties of formed thermosetting materials. For thermal stability, the lignin fragments with depolymerized structure containing lower contents of ether linkages and higher reactivity, enhancing the rigidity of formed epoxy thermosetting composites and then increasing degradation temperature [68].

Through thermochemical transformations, the formed biomass oils were homogeneous and rich in phenolic fractions (other components like furans, ketones, acids, and aldehydes from decomposition of cellulose and hemicellulose), showing the promising application in polymerization industries. For example, Celikbag et al. blended pine pyrolysis oils in epoxy resins (EPON828) with high compatibility, and obtained the highest crosslinking density after curing at the mass ratio of 1/8 (oils/EPON828) [69]. Furthermore, the bio-oils obtained from lignin fast pyrolysis exhibited more homogeneous compared to biomass oils, and enriched in alkoxy/alkyl-phenolic or BTX aromatic compounds (in cases of catalytic fast pyrolysis), which can be applied in the production of phenol-formaldehyde resins and epoxy resins (after appropriate functionalization, i.e., glycidylation) [70,71]. In comparison with lignin pyrolysis oils, the utilization of lignin hydrogenolysis oils produced by reductive catalytic fractionation has been broader researched in the recent years, possible due to the easier experimental setup to generate lignin oils, and more importantly the higher yield and selectivity to phenolic monomers. Torr and co-workers harvested the high yield of depolymerized lignin from hardwood lignin via catalytic hydrogenolysis [72–74]. The obtained lignin oils were selected as highly reactive subjects for producing lignin-based epoxy resins, which were further mixed with DGEBA in different mass ratios and cured together to generate epoxy thermosetting composites. On the other hand, hardwood lignin can be degraded into lignin oils with more G-type structures [75–77], leading to the higher possibility of self-condensation during lignin glycidylation, thus to enhance the related mechanical properties (e.g., increasing flexural stiffness and strength owing to the oligomeric structure formed in lignin-based epoxy resins via self-condensation). What's more, hydrogen atmosphere applied for lignin hydrogenolysis is beneficial to depolymerize lignin via the cleavage of β-/α-aryl ether linkages under mild thermolysis, and to further stabilize the formed lignin fragments against repolymerization [78–80].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Epoxy resins from lignin model compounds
ce:section.ce:para: Due to the structural complexity of lignin and unstable depolymerization pathways (the complex components in lignin oils), lignin-derived model compounds (i.e., phenol derivatives) with simplified structures have been used as suitable researching objects for synthesizing bio-based epoxy resins.

Eugenol is an important lignin-derived model compound [81], of which the phenylpropanoid structure shows a terminal olefin and the phenolic hydroxyl exhibits high reactivity to prepare thermosetting resins. Many studies have focused on the chemical modification of aliphatic linkages (i.e., CC bonds) in eugenol to realize its application in epoxy resins preparation, of which the epoxy thermosets showed worse mechanical properties compared to those with rigid structures. To this context, dehydrodimerization of single eugenol to form rigid biphenolic pre-polymer (Fig. 4a) was proposed as an economical and environmentally friendly approach [82]. The curing temperature and activation energy distribution of epoxy polymers showed the same trend (including a predominant ring-open curing reaction in epoxide moieties via carboxylates and further reaction of alcoholates with cyclic anhydrides during oxo-anionic co-polymerization [83]) and were significantly influenced by their structural epoxy motifs. The thermomechanical properties of thermosetting materials were mainly affected by the structural crosslinking density. Fig. 4b shows the synthesis of a diglycidyl ether of isoeugenol (DGE-isoEu) from isoeugenol (isoEu) without obvious polymerization [84]. In comparison with those cured from dimeric epoxy polymers, epoxy thermosets obtained from DGE-isoEu without any obvious polymerization exhibited lower curing temperature and thermal stability, mainly owing to the decreasing structural rigidity [84]. In addition, a different cationic polymerization process (Fig. 4c) was conducted by Kalita et al. to prepared cross-linked epoxy pre-polymer (2-eugenoloxyvinyl ether, EEVE), which was applied as a building block for preparing epoxy poly EEVE (Epoly(EEVE)) [85]. These formed thermosetting materials exhibited the similar or higher crosslinking density and hardness compared to those from DGEBA resin, showing the potential of Epoly(EEVE) to be competitive with petroleum-based DGEBA resins.

Typically, lignin-derived model compounds are substituted by inert methoxy groups, which makes polymerization reactions more difficult [86]. Nicastro et al. investigated the correlation between the number of methoxy groups and thermomechanical properties of thermosetting materials, and results showed that the increasing methoxy number was disadvantageous for glassy thermomechanical properties due to the different crosslinking topography and the hindered backbone mobility/increasing chain packing density [87]. On the other hand, the increasing number of methoxy groups in epoxy thermosets reduced the thermal energy for cleaving phenoxy-glycidyl oxygen‑carbon bond [88], thus to decrease thermal stability. To this context, several modifications have been introduced to increase reactive sites in lignin-derived model compounds, such as o-demethylation (to increasing phenolic hydroxyl content); self-condensation to form dimers or trimers (with two or three phenolic hydroxyls); phenols hydroxymethylation to form Novolac via crosslinking. These modified lignin derivatives from lignin-derived model compounds have higher molecular weight and at least two reactive sites, which can be further glycidylated with ECH and then poly-condensed to prepare epoxy thermosets via curing reactions. For example, Zhao et al. used dihydroeugenol (DHE) to prepared bio-based epoxy nanocomposites [89,90]. To increase the content of hydroxyl groups, three ration pathways (Fig. 5 ) were applied such as o-demethylation of DHE to yield propylcatechol (DHEO), self-condensation of DHE to form DHE dimer (and further o-demethylation to form DHEO-dimer), and crosslinking via phenol hydroxymethylation to prepare Novolac (DHEO-NOVO), which were further glycidylated to form glycidylated ether (GE) of lignin-based polymers (e.g., GE-DHEO, GE-DHE-dimer, GE-DHEO-dimer, and GE-DHEO-NOVO). The variations of crosslinking density in these lignin-based GE polymers were mainly attributed to their molecular weight, orientation and epoxy number. Among these parameters, increasing molecular weight, inhibition of benzodioxane formation, and increasing epoxy content with branched configuration can improve the crosslinking density [91,92], thus to benefit the enhancement of thermal stability.

Aromatic acids and vanillin are common depolymerized products from lignin oxidative degradation, where vanillin can be synthesized to polyvanillin [54,93–95], showing their potential to be used as epoxy pre-polymers. Fang et al. reported that the direct use of mixed aromatic acids (Fig. 6a) was attractive in bio-based epoxy resins preparation due to the low cost of their preparation from lignin conversion [96]. For thermosetting materials prepared from pure aromatic monomers or aromatic monomers/EPO826 mixture, the aromatic monomers blending caused few variations on curing characteristics, while the structural difference in prepared resins led to some changes on polymerization enthalpy. For their thermomechanical properties, due to the high content of short chains in thermosetting materials, the formed rigid structure with high crosslinking density led to their high thermal stability during thermal decomposition process [97]. In addition, more chain ends (i.e., methoxy groups) existing in epoxy monomers would lead to lower crosslinking density and cause a decrease in storage modulus of related thermosetting materials [98]. Through the direct coupling of 5 and 5′ positions in vanillin, the formed divanillin with absent spacers and short segments can minimize the rotational motion of the backbone, hence improving the dynamic performance of the created poly network (Fig. 6b) [99,100]. Furthermore, as compared to vanillin, the higher condensed structures (or higher crosslinking density) and more content of epoxy groups (after modification) of divanillin (or divanillyl alcohol obtained after reduction [99], Fig. 6c) exhibited their promising applications as epoxy pre-polymers for preparing bio-based epoxy resins with better thermomechanical properties.

Except for phenolic dimers (e.g., dihydroeugenol-dimer, divanillin, divanillyl alcohol), triphenols prepared from lignin-derived model compounds have also been used as epoxy pre-polymers due to the higher content of reactive hydroxyls. For example, Zhao et al. fabricated lignin-based epoxy thermosets from lignin-derived triphenols (TPs), which were obtained from chemical coupling of lignin-derived phenol/aldehyde monomers (i.e., LDPMs/LDAMs) using bridging reagents (Fig. 7 ) [102,103]. In comparison with phenolic dimers, the structural rigidity of TPs-based thermosetting materials would be significantly improved due to the increasing crosslinking density, thereby enhancing the related mechanical properties [103]. Based on the previous studies, the presence of methoxy (a typical substitution with chemical inertness existing in lignin aromatic rings) caused negative effects on crosslinking density of epoxy networks, affecting thermomechanical properties of thermosetting materials [104], and o-demethylation [89,103] would be an efficient modification method to convert methoxy into reactive hydroxyls. Besides, a renewable lignin-based triphenylmethane-type phenol (i.e., VAN-M-CAT, and its glycidylated derivative GE-VAN-M-CAT) was fabricated from vanillin, which was further constructed by esterification with chlorinated linoleic acid (LIN) followed by glycidylation (i.e., VAN-LIN-EPO) [105]. After mixing them with different ratios (GE-VAN-M-CATX/VAN-LIN-EPO100-X), the lower crosslinking density was obtained with the increasing of LIN content due to the enhanced mobility of polymeric segments. On the other hand, closed loop would be formed both in epoxy pre-polymers and adjacent chains of LIN, reducing their functionality to form crosslinking network.

Carbohydrates and lignin are dominant components of lignocellulosic biomass, which can be used to prepare furan-containing polyphenols using their derived monomers like furans and phenols (Fig. 8 ) [106,107]. The comparable study of thermosetting materials prepared from furanyl- and phenyl-based diepoxy monomers were performed by Hu et al., showing that furanyl-based one exhibited improved glassy properties [108]. Therefore, furan-derived molecules can be used as feasible building blocks of phenols to prepare high-performance bio-based epoxy resins [106]. On the other hand, many studies have focused on the conversion of lignocellulosic biomass into phenols (methoxy-) and furans [109,110], which can be used as reactive substrates in condensation reactions to fabricate phenol-furan epoxy pre-polymers, containing more functional groups, molecular weight and total aromaticity compared to the single phenol-based ones, thus to get better performance of their thermosetting materials (e.g., mechanical and thermal properties) [90,108]. In addition, this pathway (i.e., furans + phenols) has its own environmental benefits (e.g., biodegradation and less toxicity) due to the promising replacement of formaldehyde with furans in epoxy industries (the similar environmental effect can also be obtained via using vanillin as binding reagent for fabricating phenolic dimers or trimers) [111]. For their thermal and mechanical properties, the presence of extra aliphatic hydroxyl in epoxy pre-polymers (i.e., MHE, Fig. 8a) would accelerate the curing process via reducing curing temperature [112], and the higher crosslinking density would be obtained from the enhanced hydrogen bonding inter-chain reactions between hydroxyls, benefiting the thermomechanical properties [113]. Miao et al. found that both bisphenol-furan epoxy pre-polymer and DGGEBA have similar curing characteristics (basically, curing reactivity of the former was lower than that of the later due to the loss of oxygen atoms connected with epoxy groups, decreasing polarization degree, which was less conductive to their ring open reaction [114]), but the former (with enhanced molecular density, crosslinking density and hydrogen bonding) showed better thermal properties and higher structural rigidity than the later one [98], mainly attributed to the unique structure of the former containing both aromatic structure and furan ring.

Due to the inherent chemical inertness, epoxy resins have been widely used as an organic coatings for corrosion protection [115], such as metals protection against corrosion caused by aggressive environmental parameters (e.g., humidity, O2, Clˉ and etc. [116]), due to their low cost, low shrinkage, good dimensional stability, mechanochemical and adhesion properties [117]. Due to the long-period exposure, the anticorrosion of epoxy coatings will be deteriorated and needs improving [118]. Lignin, as a natural polyphenol and one of the three main components in lignocellulosic biomass, has been recognized as the largest renewable source of aromatic compounds [4]. Due to the inherent phenolic structure and diverse functional groups, lignin has been expected as a neutralizer or inhibitor of oxidation, such as antioxidant to stabilize reactions induced by oxygen radicals [119]. In addition, lignin also acts as a good blocker for UV radiation due to the large number of phenolic units, ketones and other chromophores in its structure and the combination of these functional groups with aromatic rings to form large conjugated π systems [120–123]. Diógenes et al. added acetylated lignin as an additive for preparing bio-based epoxy coating with improved anticorrosion and UV-blocking ability [124]. For reducing the influence of high polarity of lignin (caused by the presence of a large hydroxyls) on its interaction with other nonpolar polymers, chemical modifications have been confirmed as feasible methods to overcome this problem, such as acetylation due to the reduced polarity, increased solubility and biocompatibility [125,126]. On the other, π electrons presenting in acetyl groups are also capable of adsorbing UV radiation [127]. The result showed that the resultant acetylated lignin-based thermosetting (using modified lignin/DGEBA as blended epoxy prepolymer, cured at room temperature for 168 h) presented a complete absorption of UV light in both UV-A and UV-B regions, a property very promising in order to against the damage caused by UV radiation and weakening durability. The anticorrosive properties (using steel plates as metallic substrates) were evaluated by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), showing the superior performance compared to commercial coatings [124].

Compositions based on epoxy resins are the most popular structural adhesives due to their wide applications (which can bond a series of materials like metals, plastics, ceramics and wood) and the presence of highly crosslinking epoxy networks with excellent mechanical and thermal properties [128,129]. The traditional epoxy composition is mainly based on epoxidized BPA molecule, produced from nonrenewable petroleum-derived resources, of which the increasing consumption would cause serious environmental pollution and cannot meet the requirement of green and sustainable development [47,72,130,131]. Due to the aromatic structure and a large amount of phenolic hydroxyls in lignin chemical structure (which is similar to that of BPA), the utilization of lignin as a green alternative of BPA not only improves the economic benefits of waste lignin but also enhances the sustainability of epoxy resin industries [11,61]. According to the research reported by Wang et al., before lignin epoxidation, an extra modification was performed to increase lignin compatibility and hydrophobicity with commercial epoxy resins. With the introduction of CC bond in lignin structure, several improvements can be obtained, such as reducing free volume inside, more hydrophobic and better compatibility [42]. The introduction of CC can be copolymerized by the action of initiator to form double-interpenetrating network with epoxy system, and the resultant lignin-based adhesives exhibited excellent mechanical properties and water resistance. For wood-based adhesives, formaldehyde-based resins, such as urea-formaldehyde (UF), melamine-formaldehyde (MF) and phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins are the most used ones for wood panels due to the high reactivity of formaldehyde, but its wide utilization is harmful to the environment and human health [132–134]. For reducing the emission of formaldehyde in the preparation of lignin-based adhesives, glyoxal-based ones are promisingly utilized as sustainable alternatives with nontoxicity, while the lower reactivity of lignin and glyoxal led to the reduce of mechanical and thermal properties [135]. Younesi-Kordkheili et al. performed urea modification of lignin-glyoxal resins and added a small amount of epoxy resins to enhance the reactivity of curing reactions to improve both dry and wet tensile shear strength of plywood panels [136] (Fig. 9 ).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Other applications of lignin in polymer composites
ce:section.ce:para: Lignin has been used as the second most common natural polymer in biocomposites, which can be regarded as the green replacer with enhanced biodegradation and sustainability for fossil-derived composites [137]. Except for lignin-epoxy resins, many other lignin-incorporated composites such as lignin-polypropylene [138], lignin polylactic acid [139,140], lignin-cellulose [141,142], lignin-polyvinyl alcohol [143,144], lignin-chitosan [145–147], lignin-starch [148], lignin-rubber [149], and lignin-wood [150] have also been investigated. Via combining with these synthetic or natural polymers mentioned above, lignin can be used as filler, nucleating agent, compatibilizer, or coupling agent in these bio-based composites. Similarly, there would be an obstacle for their combination due to the inherent properties of native lignin (with low reactivity and structural stubbornness). Therefore, it would be better to perform a preliminary process of lignin modification to obtain better properties of formed biocomposites. On the other hand, lignin contents in biocomposites are also an important parameter due to its low miscibility in these polymers, agglomeration, and phase separation. Therefore, more lignin should be added together with some proper homogenization techniques and additives. In these biocomposites, the phenolic structure of lignin has been known to contribute to the thermal stability and char residue [151,152]. On the contrary, lignin addition makes a negative effect on the mechanical properties of obtained biocomposites [153]. The lignin addition increases tensile modulus and thermal stability while lowering tensile strength and strain. On the other hand, the crosslinking ability of lignin is accountable for the increase of the stiffness of biocomposites, of which the high crosslinking density can be achieved via lignin modification to enhance the interaction between modified lignin and polymer matrix [154]. For their valuable applications, due to its high carbon content, high thermal stability, biodegradability, antioxidant activity, and structural rigidity, lignin-based biocomposites can be further used in various fields of biomedical, adhesive, carbon fiber, reinforcing agent, foam, flame retardant, 3D printing, hydrogel, UV blocker, anticorrosion, and so on.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Important results obtained from this review

ce:list-item.ce:para: Different curing reagents exhibited different curing reactivity to lignin-based epoxy resins, such as curing temperature, total curing heat and curing activation energy.

Glycidylation conditions should also be designed as a biphasic PTC system for increasing hydroxyls conversion. In addition, solvent effect was also an important factor to avoid self-condensation. During glycidylation, self-condensation between epoxy and phenolic hydroxyl increased crosslinking density and was beneficial for structural rigidity, while blending with other flexible epoxy resins (e.g., DGEBA) or reacting with some long-chain curing agents would be good for their flexibility.

Lignin structural properties (e.g., molecular weight and phenolic content) were key factors to influence the epoxy synthesis and properties. Lignin fractions with lower molecular weight contained higher reactivity in glycidylation and co-curing reactions.

Lignin-based epoxy resins prepared from macromolecular lignin exhibited their promising substitutions for DGEBA. Lignin blending content and lignin structure made greatly influenced the synthesis and certain properties (thermal and mechanical) of as-prepared thermosets. Due to the physical reinforcement of lignin, lower blending contents of lignin exhibited the positive effects on crosslinking density and mechanical properties. However, excessive lignin addition would lead to a higher rigid structure, which was disadvantageous for flexibility, but good for thermal stability.

For lignin model compounds, due to their insufficiency of reactivity (only one aromatic ring contains one phenolic hydroxyl), several modifications were used to increase reactive sites, such as o-demethylation, self-condensation to form certain dimers or trimers, phenols hydroxymethylation to form Novolac, extra introduction of reactive sites, or forming aromatic carboxyl via structure oxidation. In addition, preparing bisphenol-furan type polyphenols was also an effective method not only to prepare high-performance bio-based epoxy resins, but also to obtain their environmental benefits (i.e., biodegradation) due to the replacement of formaldehyde with furan.

As an important raw material of bio-based epoxy resins, it is difficult to control or predict the inherent structure of lignin obtained from lignocellulose (such as phenolic content, molecular weight and the distribution of other functional groups) via different extractions. On the other hand, extra lignin extraction, purification and/or treatment would make epoxy preparation more complex. How to prepare epoxy resins directly from raw biomass resources/or pretreated ones still requires further researches.

Recently, the existing raw materials of epoxy resins such as BPA and ECH heavily depend on nonrenewable fossil-derived resources, and over 90 % of epoxy polymers are based on BPA, such as DGEBA resin. Although bio-based materials have the potential to replace BPA, their proportions are relatively low, and some disadvantages can be found, such as complex preparation processes, poor liquidity and dispersion. It is necessary to develop fully bio-based epoxy resins with facile fabrication and excellent physicochemical properties.

It is difficult to depolymerize lignin into low-molecule phenols with high selectivity, and some functional groups in this depolymerized fragments would cause adverse effects on epoxy preparation, such as methoxy. Therefore, an efficient pretreatment to remove methoxy/or methyl in lignin instead of deep structure depolymerization is more effective to promote the utilization rate of lignin in epoxy preparation.
